## 06/09/2026 09:22 — *Price of Confession* Ep. 11

Ah yes — **you mean the place where Sop (Yoon-soo's daughter) is kidnapped and held**, not the Thailand/mountain scene.

In Episode 11, Ko Dong-uk takes Sop to an **old house inside a redevelopment/demolition area**. The drama identifies it as:

> **Sarihyeon District 5 (사리현 5구역)** — a redevelopment area.

The **blue-door house** is specifically described as **Ko Se-hun's childhood home**. Yoon-soo receives instructions to go to the “house with the blue door in Sarihyeon District 5,” and police later locate Ko Dong-uk's car about **1 km from the Sarihyeon redevelopment area**. citeturn0search0

So **Sarihyeon is the story location**.

### But I think you're asking something slightly different 😄

You're looking at that kidnapping sequence and thinking **“Where was this ACTUALLY filmed? This place itself looks beautiful/interesting”**, right?

That I **haven't yet found a reliable source identifying the exact real-world filming location of the blue-door/redevelopment neighbourhood**. I don't want to tell you it's Chiang Mai/Thailand—that was my mistake in the previous answer. The kidnapping scene is presented as Korea.

If you send me **one screenshot of the wide exterior shot of that place**, I can search specifically for the actual Korean filming location/buildings.

## 06/09/2026 09:21 — *The Price of Confession* Ep. 11

Partner, **yes — I think I know the scenery you mean.** In the later part of *The Price of Confession*, the drama suddenly shows a **very beautiful mountainous, rural landscape that looks quite different from the usual Korean locations**.

That is **Thailand, not Korea**. The production actually took the cast and crew to **northern Thailand**, principally **Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai**. The confirmed Thailand locations include:

- **Baan Pa Ka Homestay & Camping — Chiang Mai**
- **Aoyama Border Patrol Police School — Chiang Mai**
- **Fang District — Chiang Mai**
- **Ban Nong Pla Sadet — Chiang Rai**
- The particularly spectacular mountain scenery associated with the ending is around **Doi Pha Ka viewpoint**. citeturn0search2turn0search11

image_group{"aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["Doi Pha Ka Chiang Mai Thailand mountain viewpoint","Fang Chiang Mai mountains Thailand","Ban Nong Pla Sadet Chiang Rai Thailand"],"num_per_query":2}

So your observation is interesting: **normally K-dramas make Korea itself look spectacular — mountains, coastlines, cafés, Seoul at night, Jeju, etc.** But *The Price of Confession* deliberately uses **Thailand as part of the story**, rather than pretending those landscapes are Korea. A Thailand production company confirms that the Korean production brought about **75 Korean crew members to Thailand** and filmed there with local production support. citeturn0search2

One distinction, though: **Episode 11 contains several different locations.** If you mean a *specific scene you're looking at right now* — mountain/road/house/hospital/forest/etc. — **send me a screenshot from Episode 11** and I can pinpoint which location it is.

## 06/09/2026 09:26 — K-dramas showing the **real Korea**

Yes. If what you want is **“show me ordinary/poor/rough Korea rather than postcard Korea” AND I want Hindi or Tamil audio**, there are some good choices. I checked the **UK catalogue**, since dubbing varies by country.

### 🥇 Start with **D.P. — Netflix — Hindi**

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["D.P. Korean drama Netflix Jung Hae in streets","D.P. Netflix Korean drama poor neighborhood","D.P. Korean drama Seoul locations"]}

This is probably **the closest match to what you're asking for**.

It follows soldiers who track down military deserters, so instead of spending all its time in beautiful apartments and cafés, it moves through **ordinary streets, cheap rooms, railway stations, working-class neighbourhoods, military environments and less glamorous parts of Korea**.

More importantly, it exposes uncomfortable parts of Korean society—bullying, hierarchy, violence, class differences and the experience of compulsory military service.

Netflix UK currently explicitly lists **Hindi audio** as well as Korean and English. citeturn0search0turn0search10

urlWatch D.P. on Netflix UKturn0search0

**Real-Korea value: 9/10**  
**Beautiful-tourist-Korea emphasis: 3/10**

---

### 🥈 **Move to Heaven — Netflix — Hindi**

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["Move to Heaven Netflix Korean drama neighborhood","Move to Heaven Korean drama Seoul streets","Move to Heaven trauma cleaner room"]}

This one may be **even better for seeing how different classes of Koreans actually live**.

The protagonists are trauma cleaners—they clean homes after people die. Consequently, the story takes you inside the lives of people whom glossy dramas often don't centre: **factory workers, elderly people living alone, tiny rooms, struggling families and socially isolated people**, alongside perfectly ordinary middle-class Korea.

Episode 1, for example, involves a **factory intern who dies after an industrial accident**. citeturn0search6

Netflix UK explicitly lists **Hindi audio**. citeturn0search6

urlWatch Move to Heaven on Netflix UKturn0search6

**Real-Korea value: 9/10**  
**Social/class reality: 9/10**  
**Crime/thriller: 4/10**  
**Emotional: 10/10**

---

### 🥉 **My Mister — excellent for exactly this, BUT not Netflix UK now**

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["My Mister Korean drama IU neighborhood streets","My Mister drama poor neighborhood Korea","My Mister Seoul working class streets"]}

If we ignored your streaming/dubbing requirement, **this would be one of my strongest recommendations**.

IU's character is poor and heavily in debt. You see mundane offices, older neighbourhoods, small homes, bars, public transport and people worrying about money and employment. It's almost the **anti-K-drama-tourism advertisement**.

Unfortunately, Netflix's UK page currently says **“This title isn't currently available to watch in your country.”** citeturn0search2 So I wouldn't send you there expecting it to work.

---

## What I'd choose for *your exact question*

**Watch D.P. first.**

Not because it's necessarily the best K-drama overall, but because you're currently asking:

> *“What does Korea look like when the camera isn't trying to sell me beautiful Korea?”*

**D.P. will answer that question much better than a typical romance.**

Then watch **Move to Heaven**. That one is particularly useful because you'll start noticing something we discussed earlier: even when Korean characters are **poor**, the surrounding roads, transport, utilities and public infrastructure can still be considerably better than what we'd associate with an equally poor neighbourhood in India.

One limitation: **I haven't found a Tamil-audio title I'm confident enough to recommend yet.** For these two, I verified **Hindi** in the UK catalogue rather than assuming that because an Indian Netflix version has a dub, you'll get it in Britain. citeturn0search0turn0search6

## 06/09/2026 09:25 — Real South Korea vs India

Partner, if your question is **“forget what K-dramas and Indian films show us—what do the two countries actually look like day to day?”**, there is a substantial difference, but neither screen image is reality.

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["Seoul South Korea ordinary residential neighborhood street","South Korea old redevelopment neighborhood street","South Korea rural small town ordinary street","Bangalore India ordinary residential neighborhood street","Chennai India ordinary residential street","India modern clean urban neighborhood"]}

### The biggest difference: Korea really is generally cleaner and more orderly

On an average street, **South Korea is substantially cleaner, better maintained and more consistently developed than India**. That's not merely K-drama cinematography.

| Everyday reality | 🇰🇷 South Korea | 🇮🇳 India |
|---|---|---|
| Street cleanliness | Generally high | Extremely variable |
| Open rubbish | Uncommon, but absolutely exists | Much more common |
| Roads/pavements | Usually good | Huge variation |
| Public transport | Excellent in major cities | Improving rapidly; varies enormously |
| Informal settlements | Relatively limited | Significant in many cities |
| Public toilets | Widely available, generally good | Much more variable |
| Power/water infrastructure | Very reliable | Depends heavily on location |
| Urban visual order | Generally high | Often chaotic/mixed |
| Modern high-rise areas | Very common | Increasing rapidly |
| Old/poor neighbourhoods | Definitely exist | Much more widespread |
| Rural areas | Developed infrastructure | Enormous range from affluent to very poor |

But **K-drama Korea is still a selected Korea**.

A drama can shoot Seoul so that you see the Han River, immaculate subway stations, Gangnam towers, designer cafés and beautiful mountain roads while avoiding industrial outskirts, ageing housing, basement apartments, rubbish collection points and neighbourhoods awaiting demolition.

Episode 11 is showing you something closer to the other end of that spectrum.

### And the rubbish you noticed isn't necessarily evidence of normal Korean streets

South Korea has a very structured waste system. Household rubbish commonly uses designated bags, food waste is separated, and recycling is extensively separated. **At collection points you can nevertheless see surprisingly large concentrations of bags, furniture, discarded appliances and other waste.**

A redevelopment/demolition neighbourhood can look considerably worse because properties are being vacated and the area is deteriorating.

So I wouldn't interpret that Episode 11 scene as **“Aha, Korea is actually like India and K-dramas have hidden it.”** 😄

It's closer to:

**K-drama Korea:** probably the most photogenic 5–20% of locations selected and framed beautifully.

**Everyday Korea:** still generally clean, organised and highly developed, but considerably more ordinary and imperfect.

**Episode 11 location:** deliberately selected from the rough end of the Korean urban spectrum.

### One enormous difference with India

India's **variation is on another scale**.

You can move a few kilometres in Bengaluru, Chennai, Mumbai or Delhi and go from a world-class airport/metro/business district or gated community to broken pavements, open drains, informal housing and roadside rubbish.

Korea has rich and poor areas too, but the **baseline public infrastructure is much more consistent**.

Economically that isn't particularly surprising. South Korea became a high-income industrialised country; India's per-person income remains much lower despite its much larger total economy.

There is also something interesting behind your observation: **K-dramas have been extraordinarily effective at making the viewer associate an entire country with its best-looking locations.** India has magnificent places too, but Indian cinema doesn't consistently package the *whole country* with the same coherent visual identity.

If you want, I can show you **“K-drama Korea vs ordinary Korea vs poor/old Korea” using real street photographs**. That's probably the most revealing comparison.

## 06/09/2026 09:23 — *The Price of Confession* Ep. 11

**Ahhh, now I understand your point. 😄** You're not asking me to identify the location.

You're saying it was **surprising to see a Korean drama deliberately show Korea looking that bad**.

Yes — that Episode 11 sequence is unusually bleak: **rubbish piled around, abandoned/dilapidated buildings, broken surroundings, narrow dirty streets and a redevelopment zone**. The script explicitly identifies it as the **Sarihyeon redevelopment area**, and the kidnapping takes place in an old house there. citeturn0search0turn0search2

And your comparison with typical K-dramas makes sense. A lot of internationally distributed Korean dramas give you a highly polished visual Korea — immaculate Seoul skylines, beautiful cafés, coastal roads, mountains, stylish apartments, spotless streets, etc. That can almost function as **soft-power/tourism advertising**.

But here they need the opposite atmosphere. **Sarihyeon District 5 is awaiting redevelopment**, so all that garbage and deterioration reinforces that this is an **abandoned/neglected neighbourhood**, somewhere frightening enough for Sop to be hidden without people noticing. The sign shown in the episode even says **“Sarihyeon District 5 — Redevelopment Association Approved.”** citeturn0search0

So I think what caught your eye is real: **for once the drama isn't beautifying Korea. It deliberately shows the ugly side of an old redevelopment district because the story requires it.**

I'd actually be interested to find out **whether that neighbourhood is a genuine Korean demolition/redevelopment area or a film set**. That would tell us whether we're seeing a real side of Korea that K-dramas normally don't show.

## 06/09/2026 09:28 — Gritty Korean crime/thrillers with Hindi audio

Yes. I checked the **current UK catalogue** rather than assuming Indian availability. For your taste—*The Price of Confession*-type **murder, investigation, secrets, psychological tension**, while also seeing less-polished Korea—**Netflix is much better than Prime right now**. Prime's Korean thriller listings I found are mostly Korean-audio only, so I wouldn't recommend them for your requirement. citeturn0search13turn0search14

### My ranking for you

| Rank | Title | Type | Hindi audio UK | Similarity to *Price of Confession* | “Real/rough Korea” |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 🥇 | **Karma** | 6 episodes | ✅ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 🥈 | **A Killer Paradox** | 8 episodes | ✅ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 🥉 | **Revelations** | Movie | ✅ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 4 | **The Call** | Movie | ✅ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |

| 8 | **Mantis** | Movie | ✅ | ⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐ |
| 9 | **Humint** | Movie | ✅ | ⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐ |
| 10 | **Carter** | Movie | ✅ | ⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐ |

### 🥇 **Karma — watch this next**

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["Karma 2025 Netflix Korean drama Park Hae soo","Karma Netflix 2025 Korean crime thriller"]}

This is probably **your best next programme**.

A man with loan-shark debt arranges a terrible crime; another character disposes of a body; there's a witness, blackmail, an accident, deception and interconnected crimes.

It is only **6 episodes**, so there isn't much filler. Netflix UK lists **Hindi and Hindi Audio Description**, alongside original Korean. citeturn0search3

urlWatch Karma on Netflix UKturn0search3

And for the question that started our discussion—**“show me Korea outside the beautiful K-drama image”**—this is a good one. It spends time around debt, ordinary people, crime and less glamorous environments.

---

### 🥈 **A Killer Paradox — definitely try this**

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["A Killer Paradox Netflix street scenes Korea","A Killer Paradox Choi Woo shik Son Suk ku"]}

An ordinary young man accidentally kills someone. Then another killing follows. A detective starts closing in.

This has the **cat-and-mouse investigation** element I think you'll like from *Price of Confession*. It also spends plenty of time in ordinary streets, convenience stores, modest homes and less glamorous urban Korea.

**8 episodes + Hindi audio confirmed on Netflix UK.** citeturn0search0

urlWatch A Killer Paradox on Netflix UKturn0search0

---

### 🥉 **Revelations — particularly close to what you're asking for**

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["Revelations 2025 Korean Netflix movie Ryu Jun yeol Shin Hyun been","Revelations Netflix Korean crime thriller detective"]}

This is **dark detective/crime rather than action**.

A detective investigates a **missing-person case**, while a pastor becomes involved. Netflix itself categorises it as **gritty, dark, slow-burn, detective, investigation and thriller**.

That's very close to your present mood.

It's a **movie**, rather than 12–16 episodes, and Netflix UK confirms Hindi audio. citeturn0search2

urlWatch Revelations on Netflix UKturn0search2

---

### 4. **The Call — strongest psychological thriller**

Two women speak by telephone from **the same house but 20 years apart**. One is a serial killer, and changing the past starts changing the other woman's present.

It's much closer to the **psychological tension** of *The Price of Confession* than to an action movie.

Netflix UK: **Hindi confirmed**. citeturn0search6

urlWatch The Call on Netflix UKturn0search6

### 5. **Mercy For None — if you want much more violence/action**

Former gangster investigates his brother's mysterious death and gets pulled back into Korea's criminal underworld.

This isn't as psychologically subtle as *Price of Confession*. It's more **revenge + gangs + murder mystery + action**, but very gritty. Hindi is confirmed. citeturn0search4

urlWatch Mercy For None on Netflix UKturn0search4

### What I'd actually watch in your position

Since you're coming **directly from *The Price of Confession***, I'd go:

**The Price of Confession → Karma → A Killer Paradox → Revelations → The Call → D.P.**

Don't start with *Carter* or *Mantis* just because they have Hindi. They satisfy “Korean thriller”, but they're much more **stylised action entertainment** and won't answer your other curiosity about **what ordinary/rough Korea actually looks like**. *Karma* and *A Killer Paradox* do both jobs.

One more useful point: in the Netflix UK pages I checked, these titles list **Hindi but not Tamil** audio. So for your UK account, **Hindi is currently the reliable dubbed option** for this particular shortlist. citeturn0search0turn0search2turn0search3turn0search4

## 06/09/2026 09:24 — Real Korea vs Real India

Yes. **Photographs make this comparison much clearer than statistics.** The important thing is to compare equivalent layers—not K-drama Seoul with India's worst slum.

### 🇰🇷 1. “K-drama Korea” — the Korea exported to the world

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["Seoul Han River skyline beautiful","Seoul Gangnam modern street clean","Seoul Ikseondong beautiful street","Busan Haeundae beautiful city Korea"]}

This Korea **really exists**. The dramas aren't inventing it.

Modern Seoul, Gangnam, the Han River, carefully landscaped parks, spotless-looking cafés and apartment complexes are all genuine.

The distortion is **selection**: dramas disproportionately show attractive locations, shoot them at attractive times and carefully control what is inside the frame.

---

### 🇰🇷 2. Ordinary Korea — probably the most useful comparison

These are closer to the places an ordinary Korean actually encounters.

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["Seoul ordinary residential neighborhood street South Korea","Seoul old villa residential street Korea","South Korea ordinary small town street","Seoul residential alley ordinary life"]}

Notice something important.

It's **not K-drama beautiful**.

There are overhead cables, ageing brick buildings, ugly signs, cars squeezed everywhere, small alleys and fairly uninspiring architecture.

But even here you generally don't see the same degree of:

- open dumping
- broken/unmade road edges
- uncontrolled construction debris
- open drains
- extreme pedestrian/vehicle mixing

that is common in many Indian urban areas.

That's where Korea's real advantage becomes clearer: **not that everything is beautiful, but that the floor is considerably higher.**

---

### 🇰🇷 3. Poor/old Korea — this is what Episode 11 reminded you of

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","image_refs":["turn0image2","turn0image0"]}

**Yes, this Korea also exists.**

The first photograph is particularly striking: **Guryong Village is in Gangnam**, one of the richest parts of Seoul. Makeshift homes and deteriorated alleys sit within sight of expensive high-rises.

Korea has poor elderly people, tiny *jjokbang* rooms, semi-basement housing, old hillside settlements and neighbourhoods deteriorating while awaiting redevelopment. OECD work has long documented housing affordability and spatial inequality as real problems in Seoul. citeturn0search3turn0search9

So what you saw in *The Price of Confession* isn't an impossible version of Korea.

---

# Now put India beside those three Koreas

### 🇮🇳 1. “K-drama equivalent India” — India's best urban environments

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["Bangalore UB City Vittal Mallya Road clean street","Mumbai Bandra Kurla Complex modern clean","Hyderabad Financial District modern street","New Delhi Lodhi Road beautiful clean"]}

India absolutely has areas that can compete visually with developed countries.

BKC, parts of New Delhi, central Bengaluru, Hyderabad's newer districts, premium developments, airports and metros can look superb.

The difference is what happens when you travel **5–10 km away**.

---

### 🇮🇳 2. Ordinary urban India

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","image_refs":["turn0image4"],"query":["Bangalore ordinary residential street India","Chennai ordinary residential street India","Mumbai ordinary neighborhood street India"]}

This is where I think the Korea/India difference becomes much more obvious than comparing tourist photographs.

An ordinary middle-class Indian neighbourhood may contain perfectly good ₹1–3 crore houses while the **public realm immediately outside them is poor**:

private house → nice  
compound wall → nice  
car → nice  
road → variable  
pavement → missing/broken  
drainage → variable  
wires → chaotic  
waste collection → variable

That's a fascinating contrast with Korea.

In Korea, an unimpressive private building can sit inside **good public infrastructure**.

In India, a very expensive private building can sit inside **poor public infrastructure**.

---

### 🇮🇳 3. India's poorest urban environments

image_group{"layout":"carousel","aspect_ratio":"16:9","query":["Mumbai informal settlement street India documentary","Delhi urban slum neighborhood India documentary","Bangalore informal settlement neighborhood India"]}

Here the gap becomes very large.

India has made enormous improvements, but the World Bank still describes urban growth as putting heavy pressure on **congestion, infrastructure, sanitation and waste-management systems**. citeturn0search1turn0search4

For scale, the 2011 Census recorded about **65.5 million Indians living in urban slums**. That number is old and shouldn't be treated as today's count, but it demonstrates the historical scale of India's urban challenge. citeturn0search8

---

## The comparison I'd make

| What you see | 🇰🇷 Korea | 🇮🇳 India |
|---|---|---|
| **Cinema/TV version** | Much prettier than average | Also selective, but less consistently “country advertising” |
| **Best neighbourhoods** | Excellent | Excellent |
| **Ordinary middle-class area** | Usually orderly/clean | Highly variable |
| **Poor neighbourhood** | Can be genuinely rough | Usually substantially rougher |
| **Garbage visible publicly** | Exists, especially collection/redevelopment areas | Far more routinely visible |
| **Road/pavement consistency** | **Very high** | Low–medium |
| **Public transport** | Extremely integrated | Huge improvements, but inconsistent nationally |
| **Private wealth vs public space** | More closely matched | **Can be dramatically mismatched** |
| **Difference between best & worst** | Significant | **Enormous** |

And this is why **Episode 11 surprised you**.

It wasn't merely that there was garbage.

You've watched enough Korean dramas to have unconsciously learned:

**Korea = clean streets + beautiful mountains + immaculate cafés + modern apartments + beautiful public spaces.**

Then Episode 11 suddenly points the camera at:

**old houses + rubbish + demolition + abandonment + ugliness.**

It breaks the visual image K-dramas normally reinforce.

### But here's the part I wouldn't reverse

After seeing Episode 11, I **wouldn't conclude “real Korea is actually like India.”**

The photographs and infrastructure evidence point to something different:

> **K-drama exaggerates how beautiful Korea is. But Korea's everyday baseline really is substantially cleaner and more organised than India's everyday baseline.**

The more interesting India problem isn't simply poverty. **India has become capable of producing extremely sophisticated private spaces without producing equally sophisticated public space around them.** Korea has been much more successful at making the *shared space between buildings* work.

That, more than the shiny Seoul skyline, is probably the biggest visible Korea–India difference. citeturn0search6turn0search10
